A Beautiful World With Cruel Roots
A forest of high castles, impossible creatures, and inherited chains.

Mystaria is a dark fantasy world of intelligent animal-inspired peoples, ancient cities, strange companionship, and dangerous marvels. In the colossal Great Canopy, noble ratfolk live in fortresses among the branches, while mousefolk communities make entire neighborhoods from hollows and miniature passageways. Beneath their homes, predatory Starspawn make the forest floor a very different world.

The Starspawn are not ordinary wildlife. They are magical beings whose immortal Astral Hearts remember their defeats, their friends, and their enemies. They may seem like wild animals, but they understand speech, have distinct personalities, and communicate through Starsong. A creature vanquished today may return to remember the encounter.

The setting's defining contrast is not merely beauty against horror. It is **affection beside ownership, faith beside hypocrisy, and extraordinary power beside desperate dependence**. A protector may love the person she claims to own. A goddess of trust may watch her followers impose hereditary obedience. A monster may show greater tenderness than an honored knight.

There is room for games and gardens, warm hearths and playful companions. There is also room for uncomfortable choices that cannot be solved by finding a villain with a sword. In Mystaria, the world itself asks whether a kindness remains kindness when the recipient has no choice.

the-empire-that-would-not-die
The Empire That Would Not Die
The First Coil fell. The shape of its cruelty survived.

Before the surviving kingdoms, there was the Serpentari Imperium: a civilization of ancient intelligent serpents who mastered immense magical infrastructure and treated other peoples as property. Naga were engineered as prestigious overseers. Other enslaved peoples carried the empire's stone, secrets and punishments.

The gods and the Serpentari fought the **God War**. It was not a war among the goddesses. The battle shattered imperial power, and the surviving peoples emerged with very different legacies. The Duskpaws broke their shackles in the Night of a Thousand Locks. The Corvyn preserved testimony through the Thirteen Witnesses. The Vren carry gifts and curses born from betrayal.

Yet the end of the empire was not the end of enslavement. The Canopy Kingdoms, Blood Courts, Naga Coils and other communities carry their own systems of service, hierarchy and resistance. Some inhabitants insist their inherited obligations are loving. Others consider such arguments beautiful names for a chain.

Almost all true Serpentari have vanished. Their enormous abandoned works remain, as do questions about the relationship between their ancient projects and the extraordinary technologies of modern Heroes. Not everything buried by the empire has stayed buried.
01_World_and_Shimmer
three-goddesses
Three Goddesses, Three Understandings of Power
Justice, willing trust, and vengeance disagree about what mortals deserve.

**Arrest**, the spider goddess of justice and restraint, believes that authority must be accountable. Her law is meant to protect rather than merely punish. To her, inherited bondage of the innocent is not legitimate justice.

**Surrender**, the gentle rabbit goddess of love, fertility and voluntary submission, treasures dependence willingly given. Her followers sometimes turn guardianship into ownership, contradicting her central conviction: what is demanded cannot be freely surrendered.

**Baphomet**, a lamb goddess who turned from forgiveness toward revenge, treats broken promises as debts. Her gifts can liberate the powerless or help the wounded become cruel in turn. She keeps exact promises while delighting in what their wording leaves unsaid.

These are not distant, simple symbols. Their relationships with one another, their Heroes and their followers produce alliances, discomfort, tenderness and dangerous compromises. Their greatest secrets are hidden deeper in the Codex behind intentional spoiler reveals.

a-thousand-ways-to-be-a-person
A Thousand Ways to Be a Person
Strange bodies, intimate families, ancient grudges.

The rabbitfolk Moontouched cannot naturally generate ordinary mana. Thornguard ratfolk have great stores of white mana yet cannot shape it; Bloomkin mousefolk can shape that mana brilliantly but lack the supply to achieve much alone. Together they create Concordance, a partnership whose true power depends upon freely given trust.

Tidekin otterfolk carry water's testimony. Duskpaws raccoonfolk search for every lock's weakness. Naga serpentfolk preserve imperial manners and family memory. Vren batfolk drink blood, bargain precisely and struggle under the sun. Corvyn crowfolk wear living magical tattoos and learn from Starspawn familiars. Rare Driders answer to Arrest's peculiar sentence.

Drakyn dragons grow through treasures truly dear to them, and must devour mana-bearing prey to fill their otherwise empty reserves. Centaurs build beautiful machines and sacred metalworks; a freely accepted riding saddle is a marriage vow. Firstshaped variants reveal that a person need not have a humanoid body to possess a complete mind.

A race is not a prescribed morality. Each has families, disputes and individuals who may cherish, misunderstand or resist the society around them.
02_Races
magic-always-has-a-price
Magic Always Has a Price
Five colors of mana, many incompatible paths to power.

Red, blue, green, white and black mana describe distinct supernatural principles. No color is inherently virtuous: white can strengthen a prison, and black can undo a cruel enchantment.

**Sorcery** uses spoken Elder Resonance and individually learned Incantations. **Warlocks** chosen from the Moontouched handle mana borrowed from others, even though their own souls generate none. **Jesters** bond to fully sentient speaking Regalia and spend real living fabric as their tools, armor and weapons. **Centaurs** use Anvilcant to create enduring enchantments and formidable firearms; **Drakyn** alter known spells through Wyrmcraft.

Some paths require partnership rather than solitary mastery. Corvyn witches borrow foreign mana from Starspawn familiars. Summoners form Accords with those creatures to bring companions to their side and call forth Named Spells.

Magic is always tied to limits: compatible color, channel capacity, purchased techniques, material requirements, finite mana, Soul Strain or consequences for the wielder. Wizardry also exists, but its spell catalogue and origins remain unwritten in the current approved sources.
03_Sorcery
what-will-you-become
What Will You Become?
A second life. A world that will remember your choices.

Heroes are humans from Earth reincarnated by one of the three goddesses into the body of a Mystaria people. They carry the **Shimmer**, a private interface for maps, messages, inventory, progression and divine quests. It makes information and travel easier; it does not erase the limitations of the body they now inhabit.

The game uses five absolute attributes: Strength, Dexterity, Endurance, Intelligence and Speed. Increasing level grants base-stat allocation and periodic universal growth, while **Skill Points** purchase specific abilities and magical techniques. Gems, mana, experience and Soul Strain are different resources.

Mystaria is intended as a **dice-free tabletop system**. No attack-roll, initiative-roll or randomly rolled damage mechanic is being inserted into this Codex. Character creation procedures are also reserved for later approval.

The most interesting question is rarely whether a Hero can become powerful. It is what that power will mean to a household, a companion, a wounded enemy, an ancient oath—or a person whose freedom was never offered in the first place.

Follow the links into the Codex to explore the world as a reader, a player or a Game Master.

volumes: The branches above, the ruins below, and places between the realms.

The river had carried a broken shackle all the way to the raft's mooring. Neris lifted it between two claws. One hinge was pitted black, the other polished smooth by years of turning under the current.

“Another treasure?” called her cousin from the dock.

“Another bad decision,” Neris replied. “Someone threw it into the river instead of the forge.”

She washed it and watched the water blur her reflection. Wakecraft had never made her an all-seeing prophet. Water remembered impressions, never the convenient whole story that judges wanted. This morning it offered the ghost of iron striking wood, a trembling hand, and a glimpse of bridges high above the forest floor.

She looked upward. The Canopy's castles glittered through the mist like jewels hung on an impossibly large tree. Somewhere in those branches a household had awakened warm and happy. Somewhere else, somebody had risen still wearing a different shackle.

Neris wrapped the iron in cloth. She could not promise that its story would change anything. But she could bring it upstream and ask whose memories the river had been asked to hide.

“Come along,” she told her cousin. “We have a very long climb.”
What the First Coil built, what the God War shattered, and what survived.

Keshi could open almost anything. That was what the other Duskpaws in her Cache said, although her grandmother corrected them every time: *Everything has a weakness; finding it still takes work.*

This lock had no keyhole.

She found it behind a false wall in an imperial ruin. Its surface was ancient and smooth, polished by fingers long dead. The black mana of Fraycraft whispered through the seams and told her almost nothing. No crack. No rust. No honest weakness.

“Some locks weren't made to keep thieves out,” her grandmother said from behind her. “Some were made to keep an owner certain that nobody could leave.”

Keshi set her paw against the metal. She imagined a row of people waiting for orders under a serpent's gaze; she imagined her ancestors learning to weaken iron one hinge at a time. She knew the story of the Night of a Thousand Locks. She had never held an object that made the story feel so recently alive.

The lock did not open. Instead, the wall moved a fraction and showed an old engraving beneath it: a coil, a crown, and the outline of a small chained hand.

Keshi took out her journal. There would be time for treasure later. First, there was a history to record.
Three goddesses, three ideals, and the mortal contradictions beneath them.

The accused had confessed. The memory silk preserved the witnesses’ recollections, and the witnesses agreed. It should have been a simple case.

Veyra, who had spent more of her long days binding liars than listening to them, watched a young Bloomkin tremble before her Court. The mousefolk had taken a sealed document from his lord's desk. The lord asked for a sentence of permanent servitude.

“Was it his property?” Veyra asked.

“Yes,” said the lord.

“And was the document stolen for profit?”

“No,” the Bloomkin whispered. “It named the people he intended to sell.”

The lord's smile did not move. “My lady, it is still theft.”

Veyra traced a thread of judgment silk across her claw. The law could explain ownership. It could even explain why the accusation had been brought before her. But Arrest had never said that whatever was legal must therefore be just.

She ordered the document opened before the Court. Her sisters moved closer. The lord stopped smiling.

Veyra wondered whether the most difficult part of justice was the sentence, or the moment one had to admit that the rules were insufficient.
Anatomy, kinship, ancestry and the costs of belonging.

The younger Naga knew the family history by heart. The First Coil had created their ancestors for administration, refined their habits, and entrusted them with responsibility. Her mother had told that story throughout her childhood.

Sevrassa was expected to repeat it while receiving guests.

Instead, she asked, “If our foremothers were so trusted, why did the Imperium own them?”

Silence flowed through the warm chamber like water finding a crack. Her aunt's jeweled tail shifted over polished stone. Her mother regarded Sevrassa for a long time, neither angry nor pleased.

“A household survives because somebody knows where every person belongs,” the Matriarch said at last.

Sevrassa looked toward the attendants. One met her eyes for an instant before dropping them. He knew every name in the household. Sevrassa suspected he knew even more about the places from which nobody was permitted to leave.

“Then perhaps,” she said, “we should begin by asking where they would choose to be.”

Her mother laughed softly, though it was not a pleasant sound. “You speak as if choice were a room we could simply build.”

Sevrassa glanced around the old imperial architecture and thought of all the rooms the family had built for centuries.
The difference between an affectionate promise and a hereditary command.

Sir Halden had remembered Pippa's birthday. He had brought a honey pastry, carefully divided into pieces so small she could hold one in both hands. He was genuinely proud of himself.

Pippa thanked him. She even meant it.

Then he placed the day's orders on the table. The last was a journey out of the Canopy, to a distant household where she would serve a cousin she had never met.

“You'll be safe there,” he said. “I made them promise.”

“Did you ask me?”

The knight blinked. In every tournament and every quarrel, he had defended his Shieldmate with sincere courage. She could shape his white mana into a wall that held against Starspawn claws. He had trusted her with his life. Yet the thought of asking whether she wished to leave him had never occurred to him.

“I promised to protect you,” he said.

Pippa set down the pastry. “Then protect my answer.”

For the first time in their years of partnership, the white mana between them felt less like a wall than a door he was afraid to open.
A second life measured in five attributes—and choices no interface can make.

Ilyss woke beneath unfamiliar stars and found a tail she had never possessed. She remained perfectly still until the panic faded enough to look at the Shimmer hovering at the edge of her thoughts.

The interface was calm. It offered a map, a clock, and facts about her new body. It could not tell her why the first traveler to see her had reached for a weapon.

“Serpentari,” the traveler breathed.

“Untouched,” Ilyss replied, surprising herself with a word she seemed to know. “That isn't the same thing.”

The traveler did not lower the spear. Ilyss remembered being a person whose appearance had rarely caused this particular kind of fear. She remembered cities, schoolrooms, arguments that now seemed almost weightless. Here, history belonged to her silhouette before it belonged to her actions.

The Shimmer marked a nearby shrine. It could show her a route; it could even promise that, at another registered shrine, travel might be quick and safe. But no part of it could tell her how to approach a frightened stranger.

She lowered her hands and waited for the spear to stop trembling. A second life, she realized, still had to be lived one difficult moment at a time.
Every color offers power; no discipline escapes its own logic.

Vaelor had been saving the red mana for three days. It was not merely fuel; it was the taste of a particular Starspawn, the memory of a hunt that had ended with an exhausted predator and a furious promise to remember the insult.

Now a broken bridge hung between him and a cart of frightened travelers. He could spend what remained on a burst of destruction carefully reshaped into a rescue, or wait and preserve the mana he needed beyond the valley.

The smallest passenger looked up at him. “You're a dragon. You can fly.”

“Yes,” he said. “And what a blessing that would be if there were only one of you.”

He measured the gap, the moving boards, the wind. In his mind Elder Resonance assembled itself into a phrase he had learned at real cost. A known Incantation was not a wish that could do anything. It would obey its own principle, his Intelligence and what remained of his reserve.

Vaelor began to speak. The bridge shuddered. He hoped there would be enough left to fly home.
A soul without mana can still change the outcome of a spell.

The sorcerer had called Nemi powerless three times. She counted because counting kept her paws from shaking.

He had a larger body, a louder voice, and enough mana to fill the alley with light. Nemi had none within herself. Her soul was an empty conduit, just as it had been on the day Surrender chose her. A small vessel beneath her sleeve held the few borrowed mana points she needed to act.

The spell moved. She felt its outer pattern reach toward her, a bright thing with a shape somebody else had built. She could not build such a thing herself. That had never been the point.

Nemi extended one paw into the narrow space where the magic passed. For an instant the mana felt like too much warmth held in a hand. The limits mattered: handling, resistance, time, distance. She had trained to respect every one of them.

The spell bent. It struck the old wall instead of the child behind her.

Nemi looked at the sorcerer. “I don't have to own a thing to move it,” she said.

He began another incantation, and she finally understood why Surrender had called her chosen rather than gifted.
What a culture learns to make of magic—and what it costs to learn another's art.

Arvenna's hooves rang against the road to Veyravel. At each ascent, seven ceremonial roads curved upward through the forge-city, celebrating the virtues her teachers had recited since she was a foal.

She had brought a small bell. It had taken months to balance, and the metal held a clear voice even in the mountain wind. A famous smith might have thought it ordinary. Arvenna had never made anything that mattered more.

Near the summit, the path narrowed between high walls. She stopped. A Centaur could pull a wagon through a storm, yet the sight of a steep drop could still make her knees tremble. A smaller Firstshaped Pony climbed past, holding an engraving tool between astonishingly precise teeth.

“You can go back,” the Pony said gently.

“I know.”

That was what made the next step a promise rather than a command.

At the First Anvil, Arvenna laid down her bell. She struck it once, heard its bright sound float over the city, and promised to make things whose beauty would never hide a weakness she had chosen to ignore.
An outfit with a voice, a will, and a finite number of Stitches.

“Don't bow,” said the coat.

Cethril froze halfway through a courtly greeting. He had been trying to win a contract, and his Regalia had decided, with familiar dreadful timing, to become conversational.

“It's a harmless bow,” he whispered.

“It was a very ugly bow,” the coat replied aloud. “More importantly, the broker is watching your cuffs, not your face.”

Cethril resisted the impulse to pull the speaking collar over his head. He knew better. The garment could protect him, disguise him, and pull living fabric into impossible shapes, but it had never agreed to be silent simply because he was embarrassed.

The broker smiled with all the confidence of a person who had found a weakness. “An interesting costume.”

“Companion,” corrected the coat.

Cethril looked at the cuffs. One thread had been cut; a small part of his protection was gone. The Regalia had noticed before he did.

He straightened. “Our terms,” he told the broker, “have just changed.”

“Much better,” said the coat.
A creature can lose its body without losing its memory of you.

Merrik found the Nightfox beneath an old stone arch. Its silver markings trembled in the twilight as it watched her approach. She spread her wings, folded them carefully behind her back, and kept both clawed hands where the creature could see them.

“You remember this place,” she said.

The Nightfox gave a low chirp. Its answer came as a movement of tail and ears, then an impression so vivid it might have been a dream: cold stone, a falling wall, a terrible light.

Merrik knelt. Her tattooed skin prickled. A familiar could teach patterns of mana through a Witchbond, but a bond did not make the creature a tool. It had its own fear, memory and reasons for waiting here.

“Was it during the war?” she asked.

The fox turned its face away.

She set a small offering on the earth and chose not to press. Some questions required a better relationship before they deserved an answer. The creature approached only after she began to leave.

A soft paw touched her wrist. This time the impression was not of war. It was of the fox, waiting, and someone finally coming back.
Every blade has a material; every enchantment has a cost.

Tikk laid three mirrors on the workbench and waited for the Centaur smith to laugh.

She did not. She inspected the joints, tested the reflected light, and asked what he had built.

“A memory keeper,” Tikk said. “Not a sword. Not a cannon. No heroic explosions.”

“You sound disappointed.”

“I sound as if I know my audience.”

He touched the first mirror. A narrow pattern of light passed through the second and fell upon the third, where he had arranged it to record the shape of a tiny inscription. The Centaur studied the device again. Her own craft could make alloys hold impossible properties and equipment endure for generations. Tikk's Orbcraft took a very different route to information.

“Does it remember what it cannot see?” she asked.

“Of course not,” he said. “That would be wizardry, or dishonesty, or a very expensive mistake.”

She smiled. They argued for the rest of the afternoon over which parts were craftsmanship and which were merely cleverness. When the workshop closed, neither had won. Both had taken notes.
